The rule under everything

The Golden Rule

Student Talk Time > Teacher Talk Time

Not a fifth module, not a phase, not a skill. This is the question running underneath every single lesson, in every phase, in every skill.

"Right now, could the student be talking instead of me?"
Every lesson, every skill

The 3-phase lesson flow

Opens, builds, lands. When a lesson "doesn't flow", it's almost always because one of these got skipped.

Flow's job here: keeping these three phases connected, with no choppy transitions. One phase should lead into the next, not restart from zero.

Pre

Context

What we're talking about, why, what they already know. Warm up before you demand.

While

Guided practice

The student uses the language with support. Give structure, don't do the work for them.

Post

Free production

The student uses it without a safety net. This is where you actually see if it stuck.

The two phases teachers skip most: Context (thrown straight into practice without knowing why) and Free production (the lesson ends at guided practice, the student never uses it on their own).

Never changes

The EIC Core

Six things that stay fixed no matter who's teaching, or which class it is. Everything else, your voice, your humor, your own way of explaining, is yours to bring in.

1

Contextualize

Ground it in something real before naming the rule.

2

Student Talk Time

They talk more than you, always.

3

Flow

No choppy transitions, one phase leads into the next.

4

Engage

Make it relevant, make it theirs.

5

Homework

Every class ends with one, no exceptions.

6

Prepare

Every class starts before you walk in.

Your materials

Where this lives in NatGeo Life

A unit isn't one lesson, it's several: 6a, 6b, 6c, and so on. Each one runs its own full Pre/While/Post cycle. The opening spread only happens once, on day 1.

Day 1 only

The opening spread

A real NatGeo photo or video with lead-in questions. This is the one lead-in for the whole unit, used once, not something to reuse as "the Pre" for every lesson that follows.

Every lesson

6a, 6b, 6c... each is its own lesson

Every lettered section brings its own lead-in before its own vocabulary, grammar, or reading/listening. Don't skip 6b's or 6c's lead-in just because a different section already had one, and don't assume one section fits in one class.

End of each lesson

Speaking, writing, review

Most sections end with their own free-production task, plus the recycling pages at the end of the unit for spaced repetition. Don't reach it today? It becomes tomorrow's warm-up.

Audio and video live on the Spark platform, not just in print, if a track sounds off or missing, check there first. And the opening photo is a speaking opportunity before anyone opens to a grammar box, it's the easiest place in the whole unit to put the Golden Rule into practice.

By skill

The 4 skills at a glance

Tap a skill to see how to run it, and the traps Brazilian teachers fall into most.

Grammar

Structure without a memorized-rule lecture

Pre

Contextualize before you name it. Show the structure in use, a sentence, a short dialogue, before naming the rule.

While

Elicit, don't hand it over. Ask "what changes here?" instead of explaining the rule outright.

Post

Real-context production. Practice with sentences about the student's own life, not random textbook sentences.

Avoid
  • Over-explaining the rule instead of eliciting it
  • Teaching the structure in isolation, no context
  • "Death by worksheet", no communicative payoff
Do instead
  • Elicit the form, confirm meaning with concept questions
  • Anchor it in something students already know
  • Cap it at 1–2 worksheets, then speak

Listening

Training the ear, not "listen and translate"

Pre

Task before you press play. Never play audio without a guiding question, "listen and we'll talk after" isn't a task.

While

General → specific. First listen: general idea. Second: details. Never ask for everything on the first pass.

Post

Connected speech. After checking comprehension, show where words "stick together" (gonna, wanna, contractions).

Avoid
  • One listen, then straight to the exercise
  • Translating audio line by line after
  • Filling silence with a PT explanation
Do instead
  • Play it twice, different task each time
  • Show written vs. spoken form after
  • Let them re-listen before you step in

Reading

Moving past word-for-word translation

Pre

Set the purpose. Skim, scan, or close reading? The student needs to know what to look for first.

While

Let them infer first. Unfamiliar word? Ask "what do you think it means?" before translating.

Post

Beyond "did you get it?" Pull opinion, inference, connection to the student's life.

Avoid
  • Word-for-word translation
  • Round-robin reading, only one student reads
  • Pre-teaching too much vocabulary
Do instead
  • Ask for the general idea first
  • Read aloud yourself, with intonation
  • First read, always without a dictionary

Vocabulary

Teaching words that actually stick

Pre

Teach in chunks. Never "mistake" on its own, teach "make a mistake". Students remember the combination.

While

Context before translation. Define or exemplify in English first. Direct translation is the last step.

Post

Recycle in future lessons. New vocabulary only sticks with spaced repetition, bring it back later.

Avoid
  • Assuming a lookalike word matches Portuguese
  • Loose word lists, no context
  • Ignoring word stress
Do instead
  • Ask "what do you think it means?"
  • Always give a real example sentence
  • Mark the stressed syllable
